name.text: The two axes of the quadrants

questiontext.text: The Agile Testing Quadrants (Marick; Crispin & Gregory) are organised by two axes. Which pair are they?

answer.text: Vertical: business-facing vs technology-facing; horizontal: supporting the team vs critiquing the product

feedback.text: Correct — a vertical business/technology axis and a horizontal support/critique axis.

answer.text: Vertical: manual vs automated; horizontal: fast vs slow

feedback.text: Automation and speed are consequences, not the defining axes.

answer.text: Vertical: unit vs system; horizontal: black-box vs white-box

feedback.text: Those are levels/techniques, not the two quadrant axes.

answer.text: Vertical: functional vs non-functional; horizontal: cheap vs expensive

feedback.text: Cost and the functional split are not the axes that define the quadrants.

generalfeedback.text: The quadrants use two axes: the vertical axis separates business-facing tests (top) from technology-facing tests (bottom), and the horizontal axis separates tests that support the team / guide development (left) from tests that critique the product (right).

questiontext.text: A business-facing test (top half of the grid) is one expressed in terms that:

answer.text: The business/customer would understand — described in domain terms and behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — business-facing tests are framed in language the business understands.

answer.text: Only a developer would understand — described in code, classes and APIs

feedback.text: That describes technology-facing tests, the bottom half.
That is one kind of technology-facing critique, not the meaning of business-facing.
Business-facing does not mean manual; many business-facing tests are automated.

generalfeedback.text: Business-facing tests are described in terms the business/customer understands — features and behaviour in domain language. They sit in the top half of the grid (Q2 and Q3).

questiontext.text: A technology-facing test (bottom half of the grid) is one expressed in terms that:

answer.text: Programmers/technologists use — described in technical terms such as code, components, protocols and resource limits

feedback.text: Correct — technology-facing tests are framed in technical language.

answer.text: Business stakeholders use — described in domain features and workflows

feedback.text: That describes business-facing tests, the top half.

answer.text: Are always run manually by end users

feedback.text: Technology-facing tests are typically automated or tool-driven, not manual user runs.

answer.text: Only exist for the user interface

feedback.text: Technology-facing tests target code, components and infrastructure, not just the UI.

generalfeedback.text: Technology-facing tests are described in technical terms that programmers and technologists use — units, components, APIs, protocols, and resource behaviour. They sit in the bottom half of the grid (Q1 and Q4).

questiontext.text: Tests on the left, that support the team (guide development), are best characterised as:

answer.text: Tests that guide development — written before or alongside the code to define what to build

feedback.text: Correct — supporting-the-team tests guide development as it happens.

answer.text: Tests that evaluate the finished product to find weaknesses after it is built

feedback.text: That describes critiquing-the-product tests, on the right.

answer.text: Tests written only after release, by end users

feedback.text: Supporting tests are written before/with the code, not after release.
Support-the-team tests are heavily automated (especially Q1); they are not defined by being manual.

generalfeedback.text: Supporting-the-team tests (the left column, Q1 and Q2) guide development: they are written before or with the code to express intent and give fast feedback while building.

questiontext.text: Tests on the right, that critique the product, are best characterised as:

answer.text: Tests that evaluate the built product to find shortcomings, from the user's or a quality attribute's perspective

feedback.text: Correct — critiquing tests assess the product after it exists.

answer.text: Tests written before the code to define the expected behaviour

feedback.text: That describes supporting-the-team tests, on the left.

answer.text: Tests that only a compiler performs

feedback.text: Critiquing tests are performed by people and tools, not the compiler.

answer.text: Tests that must always be automated

feedback.text: Critiquing includes largely manual work (Q3) as well as tool-based work (Q4).

generalfeedback.text: Critiquing-the-product tests (the right column, Q3 and Q4) evaluate the product that has been built, looking for shortcomings — either from the user's viewpoint (Q3) or against technical quality attributes (Q4).

questiontext.text: Which kinds of test belong in Q1 (technology-facing, supporting the team)?

answer.text: Unit tests, component tests, and API/integration tests (TDD)

feedback.text: Correct — Q1 holds developer tests that guide the code.
Those are business-facing critiques and belong in Q3.
Those are technology-facing critiques and belong in Q4.
Those are business-facing supports and belong in Q2.

generalfeedback.text: Q1 is technology-facing and supports the team: unit tests, component tests, and API/integration tests written as part of test-driven development. It is typically fully automated.

questiontext.text: Which kinds of test belong in Q2 (business-facing, supporting the team)?

answer.text: Functional/story tests, examples, prototypes, simulations, and acceptance tests that guide development

feedback.text: Correct — Q2 holds business-facing tests that define what to build.
Those are technology-facing supports and belong in Q1.

answer.text: Exploratory and user acceptance testing of the finished product

feedback.text: Those are business-facing critiques and belong in Q3.
Those are technology-facing critiques and belong in Q4.

generalfeedback.text: Q2 is business-facing and supports the team: functional/story tests, examples, prototypes, simulations, and acceptance tests that guide development. It mixes automated and some manual work.

questiontext.text: Which kinds of test belong in Q3 (business-facing, critiquing the product)?

answer.text: Exploratory testing, usability testing, user acceptance testing, and alpha/beta

feedback.text: Correct — Q3 holds business-facing critiques of the built product.
Those are technology-facing supports and belong in Q1.
Those are technology-facing critiques and belong in Q4.

answer.text: Prototypes and story tests that guide development

feedback.text: Those are business-facing supports and belong in Q2.

generalfeedback.text: Q3 is business-facing and critiques the product: exploratory testing, usability testing, user acceptance testing, and alpha/beta. It is largely manual, relying on human judgement.

questiontext.text: Which kinds of test belong in Q4 (technology-facing, critiquing the product)?

answer.text: Performance, load, stress, security and other non-functional ("-ility") tests

feedback.text: Correct — Q4 holds tool-based technical critiques.

answer.text: Unit and API tests written during coding

feedback.text: Those are technology-facing supports and belong in Q1.
Those are business-facing critiques and belong in Q3.

answer.text: Story tests and examples that guide development

feedback.text: Those are business-facing supports and belong in Q2.

generalfeedback.text: Q4 is technology-facing and critiques the product: performance, load, stress, security, and other non-functional "-ility" tests. It is tool-based, needing specialised tooling.

questiontext.text: Unit tests written as part of TDD fall into which quadrant?

feedback.text: Correct — unit tests are technical and guide development, so Q1.
Unit tests are technology-facing, not business-facing.
Unit tests support development; they do not critique the finished product from the user's view.
Unit tests guide the code (support), they do not critique it as a non-functional attribute.

generalfeedback.text: Unit tests are technology-facing (written in code terms) and support the team (written with the code to guide development), placing them in Q1.

questiontext.text: Exploratory testing falls into which quadrant?

feedback.text: Correct — exploratory testing critiques the built product from the user's perspective.
Exploratory testing is business-facing and critiques the product; it does not guide the code.
Exploratory testing critiques the built product; it does not guide development.
Exploratory testing is business-facing (user perspective), not technology-facing.

generalfeedback.text: Exploratory testing is business-facing (assessing behaviour from the user's viewpoint) and critiques the product that has been built, placing it in Q3. It is largely a manual, human-judgement activity.

questiontext.text: Performance testing falls into which quadrant?

feedback.text: Correct — performance is a technical critique of the built product.
Performance testing critiques the built product; it does not guide development.
Performance is technology-facing and a critique, not a business-facing support.
Performance is technology-facing, not business-facing.

generalfeedback.text: Performance testing is technology-facing (a technical quality attribute) and critiques the built product, placing it in Q4. It is tool-based.

questiontext.text: Functional (story) tests that express acceptance criteria to guide development fall into which quadrant?

feedback.text: Correct — story tests are business-facing and guide development, so Q2.
Story tests are business-facing, not technology-facing.
These guide development (support); they are not a critique of the finished product.
Story tests are business-facing supports, not technical critiques.

generalfeedback.text: Functional/story tests express acceptance criteria in business terms and are written to guide development, making them business-facing supports — Q2.

name.text: Which quadrant is tech-facing and supports the team

questiontext.text: Which quadrant is defined by being technology-facing and supporting the team?

feedback.text: Correct — Q1 is technology-facing and supports the team.
Q2 supports the team but is business-facing.
Q3 is business-facing and critiques the product.
Q4 is technology-facing but critiques the product.

generalfeedback.text: Q1 sits at the intersection of technology-facing (bottom) and supporting the team (left): unit, component and API tests.

name.text: Vertical axis is business vs technology

questiontext.text: On the Agile Testing Quadrants, the vertical axis distinguishes business-facing tests from technology-facing tests.

feedback.text: Correct — vertical = business-facing (top) vs technology-facing (bottom).
The vertical axis is exactly business-facing vs technology-facing; the horizontal axis is support vs critique.

generalfeedback.text: Vertical axis: business-facing (top) vs technology-facing (bottom). Horizontal axis: supporting the team (left) vs critiquing the product (right).

questiontext.text: A test is described as business-facing and supporting the team (it guides development). Which quadrant is it?

feedback.text: Correct — business-facing + supporting the team = Q2.
Q1 supports the team but is technology-facing, not business-facing.
Q3 is business-facing but critiques the product rather than supporting the team.
Q4 is technology-facing and critiques the product.

generalfeedback.text: Read the two axis values: business-facing (top) and supporting the team (left) intersect at Q2 — functional/story tests, examples, prototypes.

questiontext.text: A test is described as technology-facing and critiquing the product. Which quadrant is it?

feedback.text: Correct — technology-facing + critiquing the product = Q4.
Q1 is technology-facing but supports the team, not a critique.
Q2 is business-facing and supports the team.
Q3 critiques the product but is business-facing.

generalfeedback.text: Technology-facing (bottom) and critiquing the product (right) intersect at Q4 — performance, load, stress, security.

questiontext.text: A test is described as technology-facing and supporting the team. Which quadrant is it?

feedback.text: Correct — technology-facing + supporting the team = Q1.
Q2 supports the team but is business-facing.
Q3 is business-facing and critiques the product.
Q4 is technology-facing but critiques the product rather than supporting the team.

generalfeedback.text: Technology-facing (bottom) and supporting the team (left) intersect at Q1 — unit, component and API/integration tests.

questiontext.text: A test is described as business-facing and critiquing the product. Which quadrant is it?

feedback.text: Correct — business-facing + critiquing the product = Q3.
Q1 is technology-facing and supports the team.
Q2 is business-facing but supports the team rather than critiquing.
Q4 critiques the product but is technology-facing.

generalfeedback.text: Business-facing (top) and critiquing the product (right) intersect at Q3 — exploratory, usability, UAT, alpha/beta.

name.text: Which quadrant is typically fully automated

questiontext.text: Which quadrant is typically fully automated?

feedback.text: Correct — Q1 (unit/component/API tests) is normally fully automated.
Q3 (exploratory, usability, UAT) is largely manual.
Q4 is tool-based rather than "fully automated" in the unit-test sense; the fully automated quadrant is Q1.
Q1 is the quadrant that is characteristically fully automated.

generalfeedback.text: Q1 (technology-facing supports) is the quadrant that is characteristically fully automated — fast, repeatable developer tests run continuously.

questiontext.text: Which quadrant is largely manual, relying on human judgement?

feedback.text: Correct — Q3 (exploratory, usability, UAT) is largely manual.
Q1 is characteristically fully automated.
Q4 is tool-based, not chiefly manual human judgement.
Q2 is mixed (automated plus some manual), but the characteristically manual quadrant is Q3.

generalfeedback.text: Q3 (business-facing critiques such as exploratory and usability testing) is largely manual — it depends on human observation and judgement that tools cannot replace.

questiontext.text: Which quadrant is characteristically tool-based (needs specialised tooling)?

feedback.text: Correct — Q4 (performance, load, security) needs specialised tools.
Q2 is mixed automated/manual; the tool-based quadrant is Q4.
Q3 is largely manual, not tool-based.
Q1 is fully automated developer tests; the specialised-tooling quadrant is Q4.

generalfeedback.text: Q4 (technology-facing critiques such as performance and security) is characteristically tool-based: it relies on specialised tooling to generate load, measure resources, or probe security.

name.text: Which quadrant mixes automated and manual

questiontext.text: Which quadrant characteristically uses a mix of automation and some manual work?

feedback.text: Correct — Q2 mixes automated story tests with some manual work (e.g. reviewing prototypes).
Q1 is characteristically fully automated.
Q3 is largely manual.
Q4 is characteristically tool-based.

generalfeedback.text: Q2 mixes automation and manual work: functional/story tests are commonly automated, while prototypes and simulations often involve manual review and conversation.

questiontext.text: Which statement about supporting-the-team (left-column) tests is correct?

answer.text: They are written before or with the code to guide development and give fast feedback

feedback.text: Correct — support tests guide the building of the product.

answer.text: They can only be run after the product ships to real users

feedback.text: That describes critiquing (and specifically field) tests, not supporting-the-team tests.

answer.text: They exclusively measure non-functional attributes such as performance

feedback.text: Non-functional critiques are Q4; support tests guide functional development.
Support spans Q1 (technology-facing) and Q2 (business-facing).

generalfeedback.text: Supporting-the-team tests (Q1 and Q2) guide development: written before/with the code, they define expected behaviour and give the team fast feedback while building.

questiontext.text: Which statement about critiquing-the-product (right-column) tests is correct?

answer.text: They evaluate the product that has already been built, to expose shortcomings

feedback.text: Correct — critiquing tests assess the built product.

answer.text: They are written before any code exists to define the design

feedback.text: That describes supporting-the-team tests, on the left.
Critique spans Q3 (business-facing) and Q4 (technology-facing).

answer.text: They are only ever unit tests

feedback.text: Unit tests are Q1 supports; critiques include exploratory, usability, performance and security.

generalfeedback.text: Critiquing-the-product tests (Q3 and Q4) evaluate the product after it exists, looking for shortcomings — either from the user's perspective (Q3) or against technical quality attributes (Q4).

questiontext.text: The quadrant numbers mean you must execute testing in the order Q1 → Q2 → Q3 → Q4.

feedback.text: Incorrect — the numbers are only labels; they do not prescribe an order.
Correct — the numbers are labels, not a sequence.

generalfeedback.text: The quadrant numbers are just labels for the four regions. They imply no execution order or priority — teams work across quadrants concurrently as the situation demands.

name.text: Numbers are labels not a sequence

questiontext.text: The quadrant numbers (Q1–Q4) are simply labels for the four regions and do not describe a sequence or priority.

feedback.text: Correct — the numbers are labels, not an order or priority.
The numbers do not encode order or priority; they only identify the four regions.

generalfeedback.text: Q1–Q4 are labels identifying the four intersections of the two axes. A common misconception is that the numbering is a workflow; it is not.

name.text: Which two quadrants support the team

questiontext.text: Which pair of quadrants make up the supporting-the-team (left) column?

feedback.text: Correct — Q1 and Q2 are the left (support) column.
Q3 and Q4 form the critiquing-the-product (right) column.
Q1 and Q4 are the technology-facing (bottom) row, not the support column.
Q2 and Q3 are the business-facing (top) row, not the support column.

generalfeedback.text: The left column (supporting the team / guiding development) is Q1 (technology-facing) and Q2 (business-facing).

questiontext.text: Which pair of quadrants make up the business-facing (top) row?

feedback.text: Correct — Q2 and Q3 are the business-facing (top) row.
Q1 and Q4 are the technology-facing (bottom) row.
Q1 and Q2 are the supporting-the-team (left) column, not the business-facing row.
Q3 and Q4 are the critiquing-the-product (right) column, not the business-facing row.

generalfeedback.text: The top row (business-facing) is Q2 (supporting the team) and Q3 (critiquing the product). The bottom row (technology-facing) is Q1 and Q4.

name.text: Classify a described test: many users at once

questiontext.text: A tool simulates thousands of simultaneous users to see whether response times stay acceptable. Reading the two axes (technology-facing, critiquing the product), which quadrant is this?

feedback.text: Correct — a technical critique of the built product is Q4.
This critiques the built product; it does not guide development, so not Q1.
This is technology-facing, not business-facing, and it critiques rather than supports.
This is technology-facing (resource behaviour), not a business-facing user critique.

generalfeedback.text: Load testing is technology-facing (it concerns resource/response behaviour) and critiques the built product, so it lands in Q4 — and it is tool-based.

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: security testing

questiontext.text: Reasoning from the two axes, where does security testing (penetration testing, checking access controls) belong?

answer.text: Q4 — it is technology-facing and critiques the built product

feedback.text: Correct — security is a technical quality attribute assessed on the built product.

answer.text: Q1 — it is technology-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Security testing critiques the product; it does not guide development like unit tests.

answer.text: Q2 — it is business-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Security is technology-facing, not business-facing, and it is a critique.

answer.text: Q3 — it is business-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: Security is described in technical terms, so it is technology-facing, not business-facing.

generalfeedback.text: Security is a technical (non-functional) quality attribute, so it is technology-facing; and it evaluates the built product, so it critiques. Technology-facing + critique = Q4, tool-based.

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: usability testing

questiontext.text: Reasoning from the two axes, where does usability testing (watching real users try to complete tasks) belong?

answer.text: Q3 — it is business-facing and critiques the built product

feedback.text: Correct — usability is judged from the user's perspective on the built product.

answer.text: Q4 — it is technology-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: Usability is judged in user terms (business-facing), not technical resource terms.

answer.text: Q2 — it is business-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Usability testing evaluates the built product; it does not guide development before coding.

answer.text: Q1 — it is technology-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Usability is business-facing and a critique, not a developer support test.

generalfeedback.text: Usability is assessed from the user's viewpoint (business-facing) and evaluates the product after it exists (critique). Business-facing + critique = Q3, largely manual.

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: API test

questiontext.text: Reasoning from the two axes, where does an automated API/integration test written during development belong?

answer.text: Q1 — it is technology-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Correct — an API test is technical and guides development, so Q1.

answer.text: Q4 — it is technology-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: Written during development to guide code, it supports the team rather than critiquing a finished product.

answer.text: Q2 — it is business-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: An API test is described in technical terms, so it is technology-facing, not business-facing.

answer.text: Q3 — it is business-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: An API test is technology-facing and supports development, not a business-facing critique.

generalfeedback.text: An API/integration test is expressed in technical terms (technology-facing) and is written with the code to guide development (support). Technology-facing + support = Q1, automated.

questiontext.text: Reasoning from the two axes, where does building a prototype or simulation to explore a feature with the business before coding belong?

answer.text: Q2 — it is business-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: Correct — a prototype is a business-facing device that guides development.

answer.text: Q3 — it is business-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: A prototype guides development before the product exists; it does not critique a built product.

answer.text: Q1 — it is technology-facing and supports the team

feedback.text: A prototype is framed in business terms, so it is business-facing, not technology-facing.

answer.text: Q4 — it is technology-facing and critiques the product

feedback.text: A prototype is a business-facing support, not a technical critique.

generalfeedback.text: Prototypes and simulations are business-facing (explored in domain terms) and support the team (they guide what to build before coding). Business-facing + support = Q2.

questiontext.text: A business-facing acceptance example is written before coding to define a feature; later, testers freely explore that same feature in the running product. Respectively, these belong to:

answer.text: Q2 then Q3 — the first guides development (support), the second critiques the built product

feedback.text: Correct — same business-facing feature, but support before build vs critique after build.

answer.text: Q3 then Q2 — exploration first, acceptance example second

feedback.text: This reverses them: the up-front example supports (Q2); the later exploration critiques (Q3).

answer.text: Q1 then Q4 — both are technology-facing

feedback.text: Both activities are business-facing, not technology-facing.

answer.text: Both are Q2, because they concern the same feature

feedback.text: The horizontal axis differs: the example supports (Q2), the exploration critiques (Q3).

generalfeedback.text: The vertical position (business-facing) is the same, but the horizontal axis differs. An acceptance example written before coding guides development (Q2); exploring the finished feature critiques the product (Q3).

questiontext.text: Someone claims "business-facing tests are, by definition, manual." Why is this wrong?

answer.text: Business-facing describes the language/audience, not the execution method; many Q2 story tests are automated

feedback.text: Correct — the vertical axis is about audience, not automation.

answer.text: It is right — business-facing tests can never be automated

feedback.text: Q2 functional/story tests are frequently automated, so the claim is false.

answer.text: Because business-facing tests are actually technology-facing

feedback.text: They are genuinely business-facing; the error is equating that with "manual".

answer.text: Because only Q4 tests can be automated

feedback.text: Automation is not restricted to Q4; Q1 is fully automated and Q2 is often automated.

generalfeedback.text: "Business-facing" is a statement about the audience/language of a test (the vertical axis), not about how it is run. Q2 (business-facing supports) is commonly automated; automation is not confined to any one quadrant.

questiontext.text: Someone argues "Q4 has the highest number, so it is the least important and can be skipped." What is the correct response?

answer.text: The numbers carry no priority; Q4 covers critical non-functional attributes (performance, security) and is simply tool-based

feedback.text: Correct — the number is a label; Q4 is essential, just tool-driven.

answer.text: Correct — Q4 is optional because it is numbered last

feedback.text: The numbers imply no priority; Q4 covers essential quality attributes.

answer.text: Q4 should always be done first because performance matters most

feedback.text: The numbers imply no order either way; Q4 is neither first nor last by rule.

answer.text: Q4 is unimportant because it is technology-facing

feedback.text: Being technology-facing does not make a quadrant unimportant.

generalfeedback.text: Quadrant numbers are labels, not a priority ranking. Q4 (performance, load, security and other "-ility" tests) evaluates critical non-functional attributes; the "4" only means it is one of the four regions. What distinguishes Q4 is that it is tool-based.

questiontext.text: Which mapping of quadrant to automation approach is correct?

answer.text: Q1 fully automated; Q2 automated plus some manual; Q3 largely manual; Q4 tool-based

feedback.text: Correct — this is the standard automation profile of the four quadrants.

answer.text: Q1 manual; Q2 tool-based; Q3 automated; Q4 mixed

feedback.text: This scrambles every quadrant's automation profile.

answer.text: All four quadrants are fully automated

feedback.text: Q3 is largely manual and depends on human judgement, so this is false.

answer.text: All four quadrants are entirely manual

feedback.text: Q1 is fully automated and Q4 is tool-based, so this is false.

generalfeedback.text: Automation applicability differs by quadrant: Q1 is fully automated, Q2 mixes automation with some manual work, Q3 is largely manual (human judgement), and Q4 is tool-based (specialised tooling).

questiontext.text: Why is Q3 (exploratory, usability) described as largely manual rather than fully automated?

answer.text: It relies on human observation and judgement about the user experience, which tools cannot fully replace

feedback.text: Correct — Q3 needs human insight into the user's experience.

answer.text: Because business-facing tests are technically impossible to script

feedback.text: Q2 (also business-facing) is frequently automated, so it is not impossibility.

answer.text: Because Q3 tests are unimportant and not worth automating

feedback.text: Q3 is important; the point is that it depends on human judgement.

answer.text: Because Q3 runs before any code exists

feedback.text: Q3 critiques the built product, so it runs after code exists, not before.

generalfeedback.text: Q3 evaluates the built product from the user's perspective — exploratory and usability testing depend on human observation, intuition and judgement about experience, which is why it stays largely manual even in a highly automated pipeline.

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: reliability/-ility test

questiontext.text: A team runs the product for a long period under realistic load to measure stability and failure rate (a reliability, or "-ility", test). Which quadrant?

answer.text: Q4 — technology-facing critique (a non-functional quality attribute of the built product)

feedback.text: Correct — reliability is a technical "-ility" critique, so Q4.
This critiques the built product; it does not guide the code during development.
Reliability is measured in technical terms, so it is technology-facing, not business-facing.
Reliability is a technical critique, not a business-facing device that guides development.

generalfeedback.text: Reliability (like performance, security, scalability and other "-ility" attributes) is a technical quality of the built product, so it is a technology-facing critique — Q4, and tool-based.

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: UAT / beta

questiontext.text: Real users try the finished release against their own needs (user acceptance testing, and later a beta at customer sites). Which quadrant?

answer.text: Q3 — business-facing critique of the built product

feedback.text: Correct — UAT and alpha/beta are business-facing critiques, so Q3.
UAT evaluates the finished product; it does not guide development before coding.
UAT is judged in user/business terms, not technical resource terms.
UAT is business-facing and a critique, not a developer support test.

generalfeedback.text: User acceptance testing and alpha/beta are business-facing (users judge against their needs) and critique the finished product, placing them in Q3 — largely manual. (Note: the Q2 support version would be an executable acceptance example written before coding.)

name.text: Reason to the quadrant: component test in TDD

questiontext.text: A developer practising TDD writes a failing component test, then code to pass it. Which quadrant is that test in?

answer.text: Q1 — technology-facing support (guides the code as it is written)

feedback.text: Correct — TDD component tests are technology-facing supports, so Q1.
The test guides development; it does not critique a finished product.
A component test is expressed in technical terms, so it is technology-facing.
A TDD component test is technology-facing and supports development, not a business-facing critique.

generalfeedback.text: TDD component tests are technology-facing (technical terms) and support the team (written with the code to guide it). Technology-facing + support = Q1, fully automated.

name.text: Distinguish Q3 from Q4 on the same product

questiontext.text: Both critique the built product. What separates a Q3 critique from a Q4 critique?

answer.text: The vertical axis: Q3 is business-facing (user's perspective); Q4 is technology-facing (technical quality attributes)

feedback.text: Correct — both critique, but they differ on business- vs technology-facing.

answer.text: Q3 supports the team while Q4 critiques the product

feedback.text: Both Q3 and Q4 critique the product; they share the horizontal position.

answer.text: Q3 runs before coding while Q4 runs after

feedback.text: Both are critiques of the built product; neither is a pre-coding support activity.

answer.text: Q3 is automated while Q4 is manual

feedback.text: It is the reverse tendency: Q3 is largely manual and Q4 is tool-based.

generalfeedback.text: Q3 and Q4 share the horizontal position (critiquing the product) and differ on the vertical axis: Q3 critiques from the business/user perspective (exploratory, usability), while Q4 critiques technical quality attributes (performance, security).

name.text: A type maps by both axes, not the label

questiontext.text: A test type is placed in a quadrant according to its two axis positions (business/technology-facing and support/critique), not according to any ordering implied by the quadrant numbers.

feedback.text: Correct — placement follows the two axes; the numbers carry no order.
Placement is determined by the two axis values; the numbers are only labels.

generalfeedback.text: Every test type maps to a quadrant purely by its two axis positions — whether it is business- or technology-facing, and whether it supports the team or critiques the product. The quadrant numbers are labels and imply no sequence or priority.

questiontext.text: Stress testing pushes the system beyond normal limits to see how it fails and recovers. Using the two axes, the correct placement and reason is:

answer.text: Q4, because it is technology-facing (resource/failure behaviour) and critiques the built product

feedback.text: Correct — a technical critique of the built product is Q4, tool-based.

generalfeedback.text: Stress testing concerns technical resource/failure behaviour (technology-facing) and evaluates the built product (critique). Technology-facing + critique = Q4, tool-based. Note that both axes must be read: technology-facing alone does not decide support vs critique.
